title: Indian Banks Are Offering NRIs Up to 7% on Dollar Deposits. The RBI Is Picking Up the Tab.
excerpt: A desperate play to defend the rupee has created the best NRI deposit rates in over a decade. The window closes in September.
body:
Indian banks are suddenly offering NRIs returns on dollar deposits that would have seemed absurd three months ago. And the Reserve Bank of India is quietly picking up the tab.

In the span of 48 hours this week, nearly every major Indian lender — State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Bank of Baroda, Kotak Mahindra Bank, AU Small Finance Bank, Yes Bank and Karur Vysya Bank — raised interest rates on Foreign Currency Non-Resident deposits by 200 to 300 basis points. AU Small Finance Bank is now offering 7.1 per cent on three-year dollar deposits. Yes Bank is at 7.05 per cent. Even the staid State Bank of India has gone as high as 6 per cent on five-year tenures above a million dollars.

These are not normal numbers. Three-year US Treasuries yield about 4.2 per cent. A 7 per cent return on a dollar-denominated deposit, with the RBI absorbing the full currency hedging cost through a special forex swap window open until September 30, is — as Federal Bank's head of liabilities PV Joy put it — "a phenomenal, low-risk windfall for ultra-high-net-worth individuals."

Why the RBI is doing this

The rupee is in trouble. Asia's second-worst-performing currency this year, it has fallen 6 per cent against the dollar and slipped to record lows in May. Foreign investors have pulled $30 billion from Indian equities in 2026. Oil prices, driven higher by the Iran war, have strained the current account. The RBI's forex reserves, at $691 billion, cover about 11 months of imports — comfortable but shrinking.

The FCNR window is a playbook India has used before. In 2013, when the rupee was in freefall under then-Governor Raghuram Rajan, the RBI opened a similar window and attracted roughly $34 billion. This time, estimates range from $40 billion (SBI economists) to $60–70 billion (Outlook Business), reflecting both the higher rates on offer and the larger NRI deposit base.

The mechanics are straightforward: the RBI bears the hedging cost that banks would normally pass on to depositors, exempts fresh three-to-five-year FCNR deposits from statutory reserve requirements, and even allows banks to guarantee offshore loans that NRIs can then park as deposits. The result is a leveraged arbitrage structure that makes returns look, in the words of one banker, "equity-like."

What NRIs should know

The headline rates — 6 to 7.1 per cent on dollar deposits — apply to the special FCNR(B) scheme for three-to-five-year maturities, with a one-year lock-in. The window closes on September 30, 2026. Regular retail NRI depositors who are not using leverage should expect a steady, guaranteed yield of around 6.25 per cent, according to Federal Bank.

For high-net-worth depositors, the leveraged route can deliver significantly more. Banks are already marketing these products aggressively across the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf. Punjab National Bank alone expects to raise $2.5 to $3 billion. HDFC Bank has doubled its rates from 3.4 per cent to 6 per cent.

The catch: FCNR deposits are denominated in foreign currency, so there is no exchange rate risk for the depositor. But the RBI's swap window expires in September, and rates will reset after that. The three-to-five-year lock-in means your money is committed for the full term, even after the special window closes.

The bigger picture

The deposit push is part of a broader RBI strategy. Last week, the central bank also exempted foreign institutional investors from capital gains tax on government securities, raised NRI equity investment limits from 5 to 10 per cent of a company's paid-up capital, and provided concessional forex swaps for overseas borrowings. All of it is aimed at the same problem: India needs dollars, and it needs them now.

For the 32 million-strong Indian diaspora, the message is clear. India's central bank is willing to pay above-market rates and absorb currency risk to bring NRI money home. The last time it did this, in 2013, the rupee stabilised and the deposits stayed. Whether this round achieves the same result depends on how quickly the Iran war resolves and whether oil prices come down. But for NRIs sitting on dollar savings in a volatile market, a guaranteed 6 to 7 per cent with zero exchange rate risk is not a bad deal.
